quick.summary: How to write database queries that your team can actually read and understand.
quick.takeaway: Prepare your query pieces first, then combine them at the end.

beats.line: My query has five levels of nested brackets. How do I read this?
You do not. It is like a messy kitchen.
So I am chopping onions while trying to bake?
Exactly. Instead, prep your ingredients first in their own separate bowls.
Then mix them. You should write your code that way.
We call it a common table expression.
Can I just call it a named step at the top?
Yes. A named step makes the whole flow obvious.
So I build the pieces first, then select from them later.
Your team will thank you for the clean kitchen.

quiz.question: Why is it better to use named steps instead of deeply nested queries?
options: It forces the query to run faster.
It lets readers read the logic top to bottom.
It saves space on the hard drive.
It connects to remote servers automatically.
quiz.explanation: Named steps make the code readable by defining ingredients before mixing them, just like a recipe.

quiz.question: Nesting five queries inside each other is the standard way to write complex logic.
quiz.explanation: Deep nesting is hard to read. Pulling the logic out into separate named steps at the top is much clearer.
